passage: I'm Alka, Jasleen's bench partner in Class 10. When the history tests came back, Jasleen had eighty-eight, the top mark. Mrs Dutta held up the paper and said, "Jasleen! Well, this is a surprise. Did someone help you?" A few people laughed. Jasleen laughed too, a small laugh, and looked at her shoes. Since then she's changed. She doesn't put her hand up any more, even when I can see she knows. Last week she said, "What's the point? She thinks I copied anyway." She handed in the next assignment half-done. I can't tell what's really going on inside her. But I remember her reading the chapter on the bus, twice, before that test.

qa.q: What mark did Jasleen get in the history test?
qa.a: Eighty-eight, the top mark.

qa.q: What does Jasleen's 'What's the point? She thinks I copied anyway' suggest she now believes?
qa.a: She seems to believe Mrs Dutta will never trust her work, so trying hard feels pointless.

qa.q: What could Alka do next to support Jasleen?
qa.a: Alka could remind Jasleen of reading the chapter twice on the bus and encourage her to talk to Mrs Dutta or another teacher about the remark.

qa.q: How might Mrs Dutta see Jasleen's half-done assignment, and what is she missing?
qa.a: Mrs Dutta may take it as proof that the eighty-eight was a fluke, missing that her own surprised remark pushed Jasleen to stop trying.

grounding: A classmate watches a girl whose top mark met a teacher's surprised doubt start to believe it and withdraw from trying.

passage: Monday. Shankar, fourteen, got nineteen out of twenty in the algebra test. Lokesh Sir handed it back with raised eyebrows. "Nineteen? From you? Hm." Shankar's grin faded. Thursday. Lokesh Sir asked the class a hard question. Shankar knew the answer, but his hand stayed flat on the desk. What if he got it wrong and Sir thought, 'Yes, that's more like him'? He let someone else answer. The following Monday, Shankar hadn't done the homework. When his friend asked why, he shrugged. "Sir thinks I'm a back-bencher anyway. Why try and look stupid?" He drew in the margin of his notebook the whole period.

qa.q: What did Shankar get in the algebra test?
qa.a: Nineteen out of twenty.

qa.q: What was Shankar worried about when his hand stayed flat on the desk?
qa.a: He worried that a wrong answer would confirm what Lokesh Sir seemed to think of him.

qa.q: What could Lokesh Sir have said on Monday instead, and what difference would it make?
qa.a: He could have praised the nineteen plainly and asked how Shankar prepared, which would build belief instead of doubt.

qa.q: How might Lokesh Sir see Shankar by the following Monday, and why is that unfair?
qa.a: Sir might see an unmotivated back-bencher, not realising his own surprised remark helped push Shankar to stop trying.

grounding: A boy whose high mark is met with his teacher's surprise stops answering and then stops doing homework, disengaging to avoid failing under scrutiny.

passage: Farhan Chacha stirred his tea. "Naveen, you asked why I became a science teacher. At fifteen I got full marks in a chemistry test. My teacher said, in front of the class, 'Farhan? Full marks? Are you sure you didn't sit next to someone clever?' Everybody laughed. So did I. After that, something went out of me. I stopped raising my hand. I stopped doing the extra problems. If I didn't try, nobody could say I'd cheated, or that I'd failed. My marks sank, and that teacher nodded as if he'd been right all along. Only in Class 12, when a new teacher pinned my lab report on the board, did I start trying again. So now, when a quiet student surprises me, I never act surprised. I just say, 'Good work. Keep going.'"

qa.q: What did the new teacher in Class 12 do with Farhan's lab report?
qa.a: Pinned it on the board.

qa.q: Why did Farhan stop raising his hand after the chemistry test?
qa.a: He felt that if he didn't try, nobody could say he had cheated or failed; the teacher's doubt made effort feel risky.

qa.q: What choice does Farhan Chacha make now as a teacher, and why?
qa.a: When a quiet student surprises him he never acts surprised and just says 'Good work. Keep going', so no student feels doubted the way he did.

qa.q: What might have changed for Farhan if the first teacher had simply said 'Good work'?
qa.a: Farhan might have kept trying instead of losing years of effort before the Class 12 teacher restored his belief.

grounding: An uncle recalls how a teacher's disbelief at his full marks led him to stop trying as a teenager, until another teacher's belief brought him back.

passage:
The science fair was next morning, the school hall had no power, and Jeevan's solar oven still needed three more hours. He had built it at home from a shoebox and foil, working by lantern.
At four, Mrs Elizabeth Mathew walked past his table in the dim hall and stopped. "Oh, Jeevan, you've actually made something? Well. Wonders." She laughed kindly and moved on.
He looked at the shoebox. For two weeks he had been sure it was good. Now he wasn't. Maybe she was right, and it would fail in front of everyone tomorrow, and they would all see.
By five he had packed it into his bag. When the fair list went up, his name wasn't on it. "I didn't finish," he told his friend Asif, which was not true.

qa.q: What was Jeevan's solar oven made from?
qa.a: A shoebox and foil.

qa.q: Why did Jeevan pack the oven into his bag?
qa.a: After the teacher's surprised remark he began to doubt his work and feared failing in front of everyone, so not trying felt safer.

qa.q: After Mrs Mathew's comment, what could Jeevan have done instead of packing up?
qa.a: He could have shown the oven to a friend or another teacher for an honest opinion, rather than letting one remark decide.

qa.q: How might Mrs Mathew feel if she knew her 'Wonders' made Jeevan drop out?
qa.a: She might be shocked and sorry, since she laughed kindly and probably didn't realise how much her low expectation stung.

grounding: A student hears a teacher's surprise that he made anything, starts believing her low expectations, and withdraws from the fair to avoid failing under scrutiny.

passage:
In the Class 10 room of their Guwahati school, Urmila Ma'am handed back the maths tests. "Bhupen, forty-six out of fifty?" She held the paper up to the light as if checking it was his. "Which tuition are you going to? Or who were you sitting next to?"
The class laughed. Bhupen laughed too, a second late.
Over the next month he stopped putting his hand up. When a hard problem came, he wrote the first line and left the rest, so if he got it wrong no one could say much, and if he got it right no one would be surprised. His friend Dhiman noticed he had stopped staying back for the extra sums.
At home his mother asked why he was scrolling instead of solving. "No point," he said. "She thinks I copied anyway."

qa.q: What mark did Bhupen get on the maths test?
qa.a: Forty-six out of fifty.

qa.q: Why did Bhupen laugh too, a second late?
qa.a: He was hurt and embarrassed by Ma'am's surprise, but laughed to hide it and fit in with the class.

qa.q: What went wrong in the month after, and what could turn it around?
qa.a: He disengaged to avoid scrutiny; a teacher praising his effort, or his mother talking to Ma'am, could help him believe in his work again.

qa.q: What might Dhiman be thinking when Bhupen stops staying back for extra sums?
qa.a: Dhiman may be puzzled or worried, since Bhupen used to stay for them and now seems to have given up.

grounding: A student hears his teacher's surprise at a good grade, starts to believe the low expectation and disengages to avoid trying under scrutiny.
